title: Vertical diet review
summary: NH critiques Stan Efferding's vertical diet, built on white rice and red meat, arguing that one-size-fits-all food rules ignore individual needs. He objects to the heavy red meat and dairy, the bans on onions and garlic, the low fiber and the way macros shift with bodyweight, and concludes that you should build your own diet by studying your body.
claims: A 100-dollar diet ebook is a ridiculous price; fitness knowledge should be as free and available as possible
Everyone has different dietary needs; a lifelong goal is to learn what your body likes, and by your 30s or 40s you should have about 80% of the puzzle figured out
He dislikes any diet that gives strict directives while knowing nothing about the individual
The vertical diet gets most calories and macros from white rice and red meat, supplemented with vegetables and other lean proteins
Making red meat the main protein source is unhealthy for most people, and heavier lifters end up eating even more of it
Apparently people who undercook beef suffer fewer consequences than those who overcook it, and Westerners tend to overcook
No food is universally good or bad; dose matters per person, e.g. 100 g of something may be beneficial and 300-400 g detrimental for one person but fine for another
The diet bans brown rice and other grains, some vegetable oils, soy, onions, garlic, coffee, added sugar and high-FODMAP vegetables like broccoli
Being able to digest lactose does not mean dairy is good for you; some groups like Scandinavians thrive on it, but many accumulate harm, so dairy should be questioned
Garlic changed his life and onions are a staple; they help prevent cancers that red meat and dairy may promote, so the diet removes protective foods while emphasizing risky ones
He does not drink coffee and thinks many are addicted, but coffee in equal amounts is likely healthier than red meat
Diets that are sold must look extreme and novel to stand out, which explains the vertical diet's exclusions and catchy name
He thrives on high carbs and gets fat from dietary fat; others would get fat on his high-carb diet, so macro balance is individual
White rice is not universally digestible; some people, especially those suited to high protein/high fat, get constipated from it
The vertical diet is low in fiber because it bans several vegetables, hurting people eating lots of lean meat who need fiber most
A fixed food template changes macros with bodyweight: a lighter person may hit calories with little rice while a much heavier one eats huge amounts of rice
He has not given up refined sugar and sees no reason to yet
He can eat garlic and onions without any gut issues while some 'easy to digest' foods bother him, so one-size-fits-all digestion rules are lazy
Fiber supplements are pointless; the value of high-fiber diets comes from the minerals and micronutrients in vegetables and fruit
Bowel movements should not exceed once or twice a day; abusing fiber to go five times a day signals gastrointestinal problems
The body holds onto micronutrients effectively, so you can cover them from limited sources if smart
You cannot recomp without training; on a weight-gain diet without training you may lose muscle and gain fat
Any diet that meets your calories and protein will build muscle; this one is not special
If you can get away with two meals a day, do it; you set your meal frequency, not the diet
Cutting onions and garlic also cuts prebiotics important for gut health
Brian Shaw followed the vertical diet and stopped because he felt it lowered his performance
Don't pay someone to tell you what to eat; listen to your body and build your own diet
